name: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
title: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
answer: Face replacement and digital doubles cover the use of machine learning to substitute one performer's face for another in video, or to build a synthetic performer that can be directed like a human actor. In cinematography and video synthesis, this work spans on set capture, where a stand in or the original actor is filmed with tracking markers, and post production, where a model generates the final face. Digital doubles are often used for stunts, de aging, or performances that cannot be shot practically, while face replacement is used for continuity, translation, or entirely synthetic characters. The field sits between visual effects, computer graphics, and generative video, and it draws on the same model families that power image and video synthesis more broadly.

sections.body: Face replacement and digital doubles cover the use of machine learning to substitute one performer's face for another in video, or to build a synthetic performer that can be directed like a human actor. In cinematography and video synthesis, this work spans on set capture, where a stand in or the original actor is filmed with tracking markers, and post production, where a model generates the final face. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on GPU clusters, usually with high memory cards, because training a face model and rendering video frames at production resolution are both compute heavy. A typical pipeline combines a video model for temporal consistency, an image generation model for detail, and sometimes an audio model for lip sync, and the site currently tracks 1000 video models and 1000 image generation models that can serve these roles. Storage and review infrastructure matter as much as compute, since a single shot may involve thousands of frames, multiple takes, and versioned model checkpoints. On set, the capture rig may include high resolution cameras, infrared or depth sensors, and a lighting setup that matches the final composite.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with reference footage of the source face and the target performance, captured under controlled lighting and with consistent head poses. Artists then track facial landmarks, align the two faces, and train or fine tune a model to map expressions, skin tone, and mouth shapes from one to the other. Modern pipelines often use autoencoders or diffusion models, followed by compositing, color matching, and manual cleanup to fix teeth, hair, and edges. Temporal consistency is the hard part, because a frame by frame swap flickers, so the model must carry identity and expression across cuts and camera moves.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on consent, likeness, and provenance. A performer's contract must specify whether a digital double can be created, how long it can be used, and what happens to the model after the production ends, and estates or unions may hold separate rights for deceased or represented performers. Non consensual face replacement is a recognized harm, used in fraud, harassment, and political disinformation, and the site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits across AI, a number that reflects how unsettled these questions remain. Provenance tools such as signed metadata and watermarks are increasingly part of delivery, though they are not yet universal.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward real time face replacement and fully volumetric digital doubles that can be lit and moved like any other asset on a virtual set. As video models improve, the line between a captured performance and a generated one will blur, and directors may treat a digital double as a reusable cast member rather than a one off effect. Legal and contractual frameworks are still catching up, and the outcome of current likeness and copyright disputes will shape what studios can promise performers. For now, the practical work remains a collaboration between machine learning tools and visual effects artists who understand both the model and the shot.
